The top of a near-horizontal limb thick enough to be a tree in its own right runs out of frame at both side edges, its entire upper face one unbroken sodden mattress of moss so saturated it has gone black at its base and olive-green above, the bark beneath it ridged and hard, every ridge a narrow shelf where pale roots have clamped flat.

The flank of a standing trunk fills the left half of the frame and runs off both the top and bottom edges, its bark broken into overlapping slabs like stacked roof tiles, each slab bowed outward and holding its own puddle of standing water under a thick wet pelt of moss.

The fork where two great limbs part fills the centre of the frame, the wedge between them packed with a deep wad of rotted leaf and moss gone almost black with water, the bark on each limb's inner face smooth and dark and slippery, both limbs running out of frame at either side edge.

A swollen knot on a limb has grown into a shaggy green ball nearly twice the limb's own thickness, the bark beneath the moss knotted and furrowed in tight concentric rings, the whole surface dark with water, the limb itself running out of frame left and right, both ends invisible.

The underside of a limb leaning out over a drop fills the upper frame, every scrap of moss on it hanging downward in heavy wet tassels, the bark above the moss pale and bare and soaked black where water runs along it, the limb's two ends both out of frame.

The flank of a fallen trunk too thick to see over lies across the whole frame, its upper edge a ragged wet skyline of fern and dripping moss, its bark on the near face broken into long vertical strips each holding a film of standing water, both ends of the trunk out of frame.

The flared base of a huge trunk dominates the near frame, the wood splaying outward into tall thin standing folds as if the tree has grown its own buttresses, every inner crease of every fold a dark wet channel, moss packed into each crease and the bark between them slick and almost bare.

A long strip of bark has peeled away from a trunk that runs out of frame top and bottom, the bare wood beneath it soaked to a deep charcoal-black and slightly ribbed, slippery to any root that has not yet found its grip, a narrow ledge of old bark still attached at one edge and furry with wet moss.

A limb so heavily loaded with moss and plants that it has bent downward and the whole load has tipped to one side, the upper face now tilted at forty-five degrees, water sheeting off the low edge, bark showing through the moss where the surface has sheared, the limb running out of frame at both sides.

A broad shelf of grey funnel-shaped fungus juts from a trunk that exits the frame both above and below, its upper surface cupped and full of standing water, a thick pad of soaking moss growing immediately above it and pressing down over its back edge, the bark below the fungus bare and dark and wet.

The stub where a limb broke off years ago has become a wet hollow deeper than the bark around it is thick, its interior walls furred in liverwort in a single smooth green sheet, the broken wood at the back of the hollow soaked to a deep mahogany, the trunk it belongs to running out of frame in both directions.

A stretch of trunk quilted entirely in liverwort runs out of frame above and below, the whole near face one flat smooth green sheet with no bark visible beneath it at all, water moving across its surface in a thin continuous skin rather than dripping, here and there a tiny blister of air caught under the liverwort.

Long thin hanging roots from a tree somewhere above drop past the near face of a leaning trunk that exits the frame at both the top and the left edge, the roots pressed against the wet bark for a moment then swinging free, the bark behind them dark and furrowed and webbed with its own smaller cracks.

The top of a limb whose whole upper surface is one unbroken sheet of soaking moss thicker than the bark it has buried runs out of frame left and right, the moss surface uneven and humped over whatever is hidden beneath it, the bark showing only at the very sides of the limb where the moss has not yet reached.

The bark of a trunk running out of frame top and bottom has been lifted in one great blister by something growing beneath it, the blister half peeled back to reveal bark layered in thin dark laminations like wet paper, each layer a slightly different shade of brown, the outer surface of the blister furred with grey-green moss.

A limb runs out of frame at both side edges, its upper face mostly bare wet bark scored by long parallel grooves where something has grown and shed over many years, the grooves holding thin lines of bright moss while the ridges between them are dark and slippery and almost bare, a thick moss pad sitting in one low depression.

The near face of a trunk leaning toward the camera so steeply its top is out of frame above and its base is out of frame below, the bark on its underside shaggy with hanging moss whose tips are wet enough to drip continuously, bare wood showing in one long streak where a root from above has pressed and worn it smooth.

The top of a limb so thick the camera cannot see its sides runs out of frame at both edges, its upper bark surface cracked into close-packed dark slabs each slightly raised at its edges, every crack between them a bright thread of wet moss, standing water held in every shallow dip and each pool holding a small reversed picture of the wet green above.

A length of trunk surfaces where a great slab of bark has fallen away, the wound running out of frame top and bottom, the bare wood a darker reddish-brown than the remaining bark and covered in a thin wet film, the bark remaining on either side of the wound thick and ridged and carrying dense wet moss on its outer face.

The inner face of a deep crook where a trunk divides fills the near frame, the two arms of the division running out of frame at the upper-left and upper-right edges, the crook itself a smooth compressed bowl of wet dark wood whose grain runs in tight concentric ovals, a fat plug of black-bottomed moss jammed into the lowest point.

A limb runs out of frame left and right, its top surface carrying a deep ridge of moss along its spine and then a sudden bare patch of bark as dark and wet as river stone, the moss picking up again solid on the far side of the bare patch, roots from several plants crossing the bare patch in pale flat straps.

The outer curve of a trunk so massive it fills the right two-thirds of the frame and runs out at top and bottom edges, its bark roughened into short blunt spines each one capped with a tuft of wet moss, the spaces between the spines holding damp shadow and the occasional pale root pressed flat into the wood.

A limb whose bark has been almost entirely replaced by a continuous thick growth of wet spongy moss runs out of frame at both side edges, the moss surface compressed and near-black at the base where water stands against the bark, greener higher up, and heaped into soft irregular mounds with roots threading through from beneath.

The shaded underside of a heavy limb fills the upper half of the frame, both its ends out of frame, all the moss on its underside hanging in heavy wet curtains whose tips sway very slightly, the bark visible between the curtains pale and slightly silvered where it has dried and re-wetted so many thousands of times.

The base of a trunk whose roots have not yet gone below the frame flares outward into a cluster of tall thin woody folds, each fold a standing sheet of dark soaked bark furred on both faces with wet moss, the narrow channels between them full of black standing water deep enough to reflect the pale undersides of the leaves above.
